items.prose: A lab tests 40 genes for a link with a disease, one test per gene at 5%. Treat the 40 tests as independent. The eight smallest p-values, sorted, are 0.0004, 0.0011, 0.0019, 0.0052, 0.0060, 0.0081, 0.0150 and 0.031. The other 32 are all above 0.05.

parts.question: Suppose none of the 40 genes is linked. What is the chance of at least one false link at 5% per test? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: All 40 stay quiet with chance $0.95^{40} = 0.1285$, so at least one false link has chance $1 - 0.1285 = 0.8715$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance that every test stays quiet, then take the complement.

byKey.expected: That is the expected number of false links, $40 \times 0.05$. The question asks for the chance of at least one.
byKey.no-complement: That is $0.95^{40}$, the chance that all 40 stay quiet. Take its complement.
byKey.single: That is the rate of one test. Across 40 tests the chances of a false alarm build up.

explain.text: Independent tests multiply, so all 40 null genes pass quietly with chance $0.95^{40} = 0.1285$. A false link somewhere is all but expected: 0.8715.

parts.question: To cut the chance in part 1, Bonferroni tests each gene at $\tfrac{0.05}{40} = 0.00125$. Using the same complement as part 1, what is the chance of at least one false link now? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Replace 0.95 in part 1 with $1 - 0.00125$.

byKey.bound: 0.05 is the union bound, which Bonferroni guarantees. With independent tests the exact chance is a little lower.
byKey.no-complement: That is $0.99875^{40}$, the chance that all 40 stay quiet. Take its complement.
byKey.carried: That is the chance at 5% per test, from part 1. At 0.00125 per test, the 40 quiet chances are each 0.99875.

explain.text: Each null gene now stays quiet with chance 0.99875, and all 40 do with chance 0.9512. So the family's chance falls from 0.8715 to 0.0488, just under the 0.05 Bonferroni promises.

parts.question: Using the threshold 0.00125 from part 2, how many genes does Bonferroni reject?

feedback.correct: Only 0.0004 and 0.0011 are at most 0.00125. The next, 0.0019, is above it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each p-value with 0.00125.

byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value below 0.05. Bonferroni compares each with 0.00125.
byKey.bh: That is BH's count, with a rising bar. Bonferroni holds every gene to the single bar 0.00125.

explain.text: Bonferroni uses one bar for all 40 genes. Two p-values, 0.0004 and 0.0011, fall under it, so it rejects 2.

parts.question: BH at $q = 0.05$ compares the $k$-th smallest p-value with $0.00125k$, $k$ times the threshold from part 2. It rejects every rank up to the largest one under its bar. How many genes does BH reject?

feedback.correct: Ranks 1 to 3 pass, rank 4 fails (0.0052 against 0.005), and rank 5 passes (0.0060 against 0.00625). No rank from 6 on passes, so BH rejects 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the largest rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le 0.00125k$, then reject ranks 1 to $k$.

byKey.first-fail: You stopped at rank 4, where 0.0052 is above 0.005. BH keeps going: rank 5, 0.0060, is under 0.00625.
byKey.bonferroni: That is Bonferroni's count. BH's bar rises with the rank: 0.00125, 0.0025, 0.00375 and so on.
byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value below 0.05. BH's bars for ranks 1 to 8 run from 0.00125 to 0.01.

explain.text: The bars for ranks 1 to 8 are 0.00125 to 0.01 in steps of 0.00125. The largest rank under its bar is 5, so BH rejects the five smallest, rank 4 included.

parts.question: Using parts 2 to 4, which statement about the two lists is right?

options.text: Bonferroni's 2 keep the chance of any false link near 5%; BH's 5 keep the expected share of false links at most 5%
Both lists keep the chance of any false link at 5%, so the longer list is better
options.why: BH controls the false discovery rate, an average share. The chance of at least one false link among BH's 5 can be higher than 5%.

options.text: Each of BH's 5 genes is linked with chance 95%
options.why: BH bounds an average share of false links. It says nothing about the chance for one gene.

options.text: Bonferroni is wrong here, as the tests are independent
options.why: Bonferroni holds for any dependence, independence included. Part 2 shows its family chance is 0.0488.

feedback.correct: Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate, 0.0488 here. BH controls the false discovery rate, so it can afford a longer list.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what each method promises: a chance of any false link, or an average share.

byKey.same: BH controls the false discovery rate, an average share. The chance of at least one false link among BH's 5 can be higher than 5%.
byKey.bh-each: BH bounds an average share of false links. It says nothing about the chance for one gene.
byKey.bonf-wrong: Bonferroni holds for any dependence, independence included. Part 2 shows its family chance is 0.0488.

explain.text: Bonferroni holds the chance of even one false link at about 5%, which costs power. BH lets a few false links in, on average at most 5% of its list, and finds more.

items.prose: A pension consultant screens 8 fund managers with independent track records. She tests each annualised Sharpe ratio against 0, one-sided, and uses BH to hold the false discovery rate at 10%. Manager H has a Sharpe ratio of 0.9 over 9 years.

parts.question: What is manager H's $t$ statistic? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by the square root of the years.

byKey.over-root: You divided by $\sqrt 9$. The standard error of a Sharpe ratio is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt T}$, so $t$ multiplies by $\sqrt T$.
byKey.times-t: You multiplied by 9 years. The $t$ statistic grows with $\sqrt T = 3$.

explain.text: Over 9 years the Sharpe ratio has standard error $\tfrac{1}{3}$. So 0.9 sits $0.9 \times 3 = 2.7$ standard errors above 0.

parts.question: Using $t = 2.7$ from part 1 and $\Phi(2.7) = 0.9965$, what is H's one-sided p-value? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the upper tail beyond $t = 2.7$.

byKey.two-sided: You doubled the tail. Her test asks only whether the Sharpe ratio is above 0.
byKey.lower: That is the area below 2.7. The one-sided p-value is the area above it.

explain.text: The upper tail beyond 2.7 holds 0.0035. A manager with no skill would show a record this good fewer than 4 times in 1,000.

parts.question: The other seven p-values are 0.0006, 0.014, 0.052, 0.058, 0.09, 0.31 and 0.62. With H's p-value from part 2, BH at $q = 0.10$ compares the $k$-th smallest with $\tfrac{0.10k}{8} = 0.0125k$. How many managers does it reject?

feedback.correct: Sorted: 0.0006, 0.0035, 0.014, 0.052, 0.058. Ranks 1 to 3 pass, and rank 4 fails (0.052 against 0.05). Rank 5 passes (0.058 against 0.0625), and no later rank does, so BH rejects 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sort the eight p-values, then find the largest rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le 0.0125k$.

byKey.first-fail: You stopped at rank 4, where 0.052 is above 0.05. BH keeps going: rank 5, 0.058, is under 0.0625.
byKey.bonferroni: Two is what Bonferroni at 0.0125 keeps, and what BH gives if H's p is taken as 0.9965. With p = 0.0035, the largest rank under its bar is 5.
byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value up to 0.10. BH's bar for rank $k$ is only $0.0125k$.

explain.text: H's 0.0035 sorts second. The largest rank under its bar is 5, so BH backs five managers, the one at rank 4 included.

items.prose: An online shop tests 25 new checkout pages against its current page, each with a two-sided test on the same month of traffic. The best page has p = 0.004. Suppose no page truly differs, and treat the 25 tests as independent.

parts.question: What is the chance that the smallest of 25 such p-values is at most 0.004? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: All 25 are above 0.004 with chance $0.996^{25} = 0.9047$, so the smallest is at most 0.004 with chance $1 - 0.9047 = 0.0953$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The smallest p-value is at most 0.004 exactly when at least one is.

byKey.single: That is the chance for one page fixed in advance. The best of 25 is at most 0.004 when any one of them is.
byKey.bonferroni: That is $25 \times 0.004$, the union bound. With independent tests the exact chance is $1 - 0.996^{25}$.
byKey.no-complement: That is $0.996^{25}$, the chance that all 25 are above 0.004. Take its complement.

explain.text: Each noise p-value is above 0.004 with chance 0.996, and all 25 are with chance 0.9047. So the chance of a best this small is $1 - 0.9047 = 0.0953$, about once in 10 months.

parts.question: Part 1's chance is $1 - (1 - p)^{25}$ for a best p-value of $p$. How small must $p$ be for that chance to be at most 0.05? Give 6 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $(1 - p)^{25} = 0.95$ and solve for $p$.

byKey.bonferroni: That is Bonferroni's $\tfrac{0.05}{25}$, which is a little stricter. Solving $1 - (1 - p)^{25} = 0.05$ exactly gives $1 - 0.95^{1/25}$.
byKey.no-root: You solved $1 - p = 0.95$, leaving out the power. Take the 25th root: $1 - p = 0.95^{1/25}$.
byKey.power-25: That is $1 - 0.95^{25}$. The 25 belongs in a root: $p = 1 - 0.95^{1/25}$.

explain.text: This is the Šidák threshold for 25 tests, 0.002050. The best page's 0.004 is about twice it, so the month's data alone are not evidence.

parts.question: Using parts 1 and 2: the best page's 0.004 is above 0.002050. Which next step is honest?

options.text: Fix the best page in advance, run it once on next month's traffic, and judge it at 5%
Rerun all 25 pages on next month's traffic and report the best again
options.why: That is a new family of 25. Its best page is luck as often as before.

options.text: Report the page, since 0.004 is below 0.05
options.why: 0.004 is the best of 25. Part 1 shows luck gives a best this small almost one month in 10.

options.text: Report that only 5 pages were tried, so the threshold is 0.01
options.why: The count is what was tried, not what is reported. Hiding 20 tests is data snooping.

feedback.correct: A single test fixed before the data needs no correction. The month that chose the page cannot also judge it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which step leaves a test that the data did not help to choose.

byKey.retest-all: That is a new family of 25. Its best page is luck as often as before.
byKey.report: 0.004 is the best of 25. Part 1 shows luck gives a best this small almost one month in 10.
byKey.fewer: The count is what was tried, not what is reported. Hiding 20 tests is data snooping.

explain.text: The first month did the choosing, so it is spent as evidence. One pre-set test on fresh data counts as one test, judged at 5%.

parts.question: Following part 3, the best page alone gets p = 0.03 next month. Suppose instead the shop had rerun all 25 pages and kept the best. What is the chance that noise gives at least one p-value of 0.03 or less? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. As in part 1, take the complement of all 25 staying above 0.03.

byKey.single: That is the chance for the one pre-set page. With 25 reruns, any of them can give 0.03 or less.
byKey.bonferroni: That is $25 \times 0.03$, the union bound. With independent tests the exact chance is $1 - 0.97^{25}$.
byKey.no-complement: That is $0.97^{25}$, the chance that all 25 are above 0.03. Take its complement.

explain.text: Kept as the best of 25, a p of 0.03 would come from noise more often than not: 0.5330. Fixed in advance, the same 0.03 is a pass at 5%.

items.prose: A medical field has tested 400 candidate biomarkers, each with a two-sided $z$ test. Suppose 380 have no effect and 20 have a real one. A real biomarker passes $|z| > 2$ with chance 0.9 and $|z| > 3$ with chance 0.6. For a null, $P(|Z| > 2) = 0.0455$ and $P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027$.

parts.question: How many false finds does the field expect at the bar $|z| > 2$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the number of nulls by the chance that one passes.

byKey.all-400: You multiplied all 400 by 0.0455. Only the 380 with no effect can give a false find.
byKey.one-sided: You used one tail, 0.02275. The test is two-sided, so a null passes with chance 0.0455.

explain.text: Each of the 380 nulls passes with chance 0.0455, and expectations add: $380 \times 0.0455 = 17.29$ false finds.

parts.question: Using 17.29 false finds from part 1, what share of all finds at $|z| > 2$ are false? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the false finds by all the finds, false and real.

byKey.true-share: That is the share of finds that are real. The question asks for the false share, $\tfrac{17.29}{35.29}$.
byKey.over-400: You divided by all 400 biomarkers. The share is out of the finds, $17.29 + 18$.
byKey.no-power: You counted all 20 real biomarkers as finds. With power 0.9, only 18 of them pass.

explain.text: At $|z| > 2$ the field expects 35.29 finds, of which 17.29 are false: a share of 0.490. Nulls are so many that their small pass rate adds up.

parts.question: Now raise the bar to $|z| > 3$. How many false finds does the field expect? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the 380 nulls by 0.0027.

byKey.all-400: You multiplied all 400 by 0.0027. Only the 380 nulls can give a false find.
byKey.old-bar: That is the count at the bar of 2, from part 1. At 3 a null passes with chance 0.0027.

explain.text: A bar of 3 lets a null through with chance 0.0027. So 380 nulls give 1.026 false finds on average, down from 17.29.

parts.question: Using 1.026 false finds from part 3, what share of all finds at $|z| > 3$ are false? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the real finds at the new power, then divide the false finds by all finds.

byKey.old-power: You kept the power at 0.9. At the higher bar a real biomarker passes with chance 0.6, so there are 12 real finds.
byKey.true-share: That is the share of finds that are real. The question asks for the false share.
byKey.carried: You used 1.08 false finds, from all 400. With 1.026 the share is $\tfrac{1.026}{13.026} \approx 0.079$.

explain.text: The stricter bar cuts false finds by a factor of about 17. Real finds fall only from 18 to 12, so the false share drops from 0.490 to 0.079.

parts.question: Using parts 2 and 4, what does the bar of 3 do for this field?

options.text: It cuts the false share of finds from about a half to under a tenth, but misses 40% of real effects
It removes false finds at no cost, so a higher bar is always better
options.why: Power falls from 0.9 to 0.6: the field now misses 8 of its 20 real effects, against 2 before.

options.text: It holds the chance of any false find at 5%
options.why: With 380 nulls at 0.0027 each, the chance of at least one false find is about 0.64. A fixed bar does not hold that chance down when hundreds of nulls are tested.

options.text: Nothing changes, since each test is still a 5% test
options.why: At $|z| > 3$ each null passes with chance 0.0027, not 0.05. That is what cuts the false finds.

feedback.correct: False finds fall from 17.29 to 1.026, and the false share from 0.490 to 0.079. The price is power: 12 real finds instead of 18.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the false share and the real finds at the two bars.

byKey.free: Power falls from 0.9 to 0.6: the field now misses 8 of its 20 real effects, against 2 before.
byKey.fwer: With 380 nulls at 0.0027 each, the chance of at least one false find is about 0.64. A fixed bar does not hold that chance down when hundreds of nulls are tested.
byKey.same: At $|z| > 3$ each null passes with chance 0.0027, not 0.05. That is what cuts the false finds.

explain.text: A field that tests hundreds of ideas makes most of its false finds at the usual bar. Raising it to 3 trades some power for a list that is mostly real.
